428.title: The sky is the platter
428.hook: the sky is the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls: creation performs the aarti (Dhanasri M1, ang 13)
428.carry: you don't light it, you notice it
428.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn nightly within Kirtan Sohila, and gurdwaras also sing it on its own in the evening as the Aarti, usually without lamps, while a few historic gurdwaras also keep a lamp ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gagan, the sky; your line was gagan mai thaal. Today, what the platter is for.
screen: `GAGAN MAI THAAL — THE SKY, A PLATTER.`

segments.voice: Evening at a Hindu temple. The bells start. A priest lifts a brass tray of small flames and moves it in slow circles before the image of the deity. Incense curls up. Someone waves a fan of white hair. Flowers lie heaped at the front. People sing, clap, reach toward the flames and draw the warmth back over their eyes. That's an aarti. Sohila's third hymn takes the items on that tray and finds each one, much larger, somewhere in the world.
screen: `A BRASS TRAY OF FLAMES.` → `INCENSE, A FAN, FLOWERS.` → `EVERY ITEM, FOUND IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Aarti is the waving of lamps, a way of honoring what is dear by circling light before it. Now walk through the hymn with the tray in mind. The platter: the sky. The lamps: the sun and the moon. Then: taarika mandal janak moti, the circles of stars are like pearls scattered across it. More items follow, the incense, the fan, the flowers; we'll take those tomorrow. Then the refrain. In paraphrase: what a wonderful aarti this is, O Destroyer of fear; this is Your aarti. And the unstruck sound, the music no hand plays, sounds like the temple drums. So who is performing the aarti? Not a priest. Creation itself. In the hymn, the whole universe, every evening, lifts its lamps toward the One. In Sikh practice the hymn itself is sung as the aarti, with no tray and no flames: the sound is the offering. A few historic gurdwaras also keep an evening ceremony with lamps alongside the singing, and Sikhs differ on that practice. Both share the line's big picture: the offering is already happening, all around, all the time. You don't light it. You notice it.
screen: `AARTI: CIRCLING LIGHT IN HONOR.` · `SKY, SUN AND MOON, STARS AS PEARLS.` · `WHAT A WONDERFUL AARTI THIS IS.` · `CREATION ITSELF IS OFFERING.` · then, large: `THE SKY IS THE PLATTER.`

segments.voice: Find the sky, through a window or outside: the moon, one star, the orange glow of a city night, or the daytime blue as it is. Picture it as a tray held up in honor, and yourself at the edge of the crowd beneath it. If you pray, say Waheguru once.
Aarti. The offering of circling lamps; in Sohila's third hymn, the aarti the whole creation performs, with the sky as its platter.

429.title: The wind as incense
429.hook: tradition sets this hymn at Puri, where Nanak saw a temple aarti and pointed to the one the universe performs
429.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn nightly in Kirtan Sohila and sing it in gurdwaras as the Aarti; the story of Guru Nanak at Puri is often told alongside it, especially at gurdwara evening programs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, aarti; your line was you don't light it, you notice it. Today, the story Sikhs tell about where this hymn was first sung.
screen: `AARTI — YOU DON'T LIGHT IT, YOU NOTICE IT.`

segments.voice: The east coast of India, on the Bay of Bengal. A town called Puri, home to the great temple of Jagannath, Lord of the World. Pilgrims still walk there. The janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak's life, say he came here on his long journeys with his companion Mardana, the musician who played the rabab. Evening came, and the temple's aarti began: lamps on golden trays, incense, bells, crowds. And the stories say Guru Nanak stood quietly and didn't join in.
screen: `PURI, ON THE BAY OF BENGAL.` → `NANAK AND MARDANA ARRIVE.` → `THE EVENING AARTI BEGINS.`

segments.voice: In one telling, someone notices the visitor standing apart and asks why. In reply, Guru Nanak asks Mardana to play, and he sings: the sky is the platter, the sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls. The fragrant breeze is the incense, the wind is the fan, the forests are the flowers. What a wonderful aarti this is. The aarti, he says, has been going on the whole time. It's just bigger than the temple. Hold this story as tradition. The hymn itself doesn't name Puri, and the janamsakhis were written down after Guru Nanak's lifetime and don't always agree in detail. What the hymn does say, in its later verses, turns the picture inside out. In paraphrase: You have thousands of eyes, and yet no eye; thousands of forms, and yet not one form; thousands of feet, yet no foot; thousands of noses, yet no nose. And then: within everything is a light, and that light is You. By that light, all are lit. So the wind isn't only incense. The wind, the stars, the forests, the people at the temple, the people standing apart: all lit by the same light. The story, as Sikhs tell it, isn't about scorning anybody's lamps. It widens the circle until the whole world is inside the offering, the priests, the pilgrims and the two travelers too.

segments.voice: Open a window, step outside, or just breathe in slowly where you are: cut grass, rain, someone's cooking, the dry air of a vent. Whatever it is, let it be the incense in the hymn, carried to you on the wind. Breathe out slowly, and if you pray, say Waheguru on the out-breath.

430.title: Hymn 4, sound: kaam karodh
430.hook: kaam karodh nagar bahu bhariaa (Gauri Purbi M4, ang 13)
430.howItsDone: This is the fourth of the five hymns Sikhs recite every night in Kirtan Sohila; it is Guru Ram Das's, and it follows the three hymns of Guru Nanak.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pavan, the wind; your line was the whole world offering. Today the mood changes: hymn four.

A new voice enters Sohila tonight. The first three hymns were Guru Nanak's. The fourth is by Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, whom Sikhs remember as the founder of the town that grew into Amritsar. Someone who founds a town learns how one fills up, street by street. So it fits that his hymn is about a crowded town. Only this town isn't on any map. It's a body at the end of a long day, with whatever it's still carrying.
screen: `A NEW VOICE: GURU RAM DAS.` → `A TOWN, AND A CROWDED ONE.` → `THE FIRST LINE IS A WARNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the line: kaam karodh nagar bahu bhariaa. Word by word. Kaam: desire that has run out of control, lust, craving. Karodh: anger. Nagar: a town, a city. Bahu: very much. Bhariaa: filled. So: the city is crammed with desire and anger. The city is the body, and the mind that lives in it, its streets full of two restless characters who never seem to sleep. Then the line finishes, and the warning becomes a hope. In paraphrase: meeting the holy, they are broken to pieces. The holy here is saadhoo, the person who has truly given themselves to God, and some readers hear in it the sangat, the company of people who sing God's praise together. So the hymn doesn't pretend the city is quiet. It names the crowd, and it names what breaks it up. The hymn is in Raag Gauri Purbi, on Ang 13, right after Guru Nanak's three. Listen to its sound: kaam and karodh both open on a hard k. The line begins with a jolt, like a door banged at night, hard to sleep through. Tomorrow, the rest of the city's residents. Today, two loud names, a crowded town, and the promise that the crowd can be broken.

431.title: A city full of thieves
431.hook: the body is a city crowded with lust and anger; meeting the holy, they are broken (Gauri Purbi M4, ang 13)
431.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn every night in Kirtan Sohila, and the five thieves (kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, hankaar) are a staple of Sikh teaching, answered by Naam, seva and the sangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, krodh, anger; your line was kaam karodh, desire and anger. Today, the whole city.

Lights off. Phone face down. The body exhausted, the mind wide awake. It replays an argument from lunch. It scrolls through something it wants and can't have. It drafts the perfect reply that will never be sent. The room is quiet, but the city inside is not, and none of the crowd got the memo that it's bedtime. Sohila's fourth hymn is recited at exactly that hour, and it names two of the loudest.
screen: `THE ROOM IS QUIET.` → `THE CITY INSIDE IS NOT.` → `TWO OF THEM HAVE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Another hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib names the whole crowd plainly: in this body live five thieves, chor. Kaam, desire out of control. Krodh, anger. Lobh, greed. Moh, clinging attachment. And hankaar, ego, pride. That hymn says they plunder the nectar inside; in plain terms, they steal attention, peace, the hours meant for something better. This hymn names the first two, crowding the city. Then it shows the deeper problem. In paraphrase: the faithless one never tastes the sweetness of God; inside them is the thorn of ego, and the more they walk, the more it pricks. Anyone with a splinter in their foot knows that picture: you can keep walking, but every step hurts, and the cause is inside. So how is the city cleared? Not by force. The hymn's answer is humility and company. In paraphrase: greet the holy with joined palms, a great merit; bow before them, a great merit. Meeting the holy, desire and anger break apart. And God's humble servants merge in the Name, and the pain of birth and death is broken. For Sikhs, the holy company is sangat, people gathered to sing God's praise. The hymn doesn't picture anyone fighting the thieves alone in the dark. It pictures joined palms, a bowed head, and good company. The city clears because better company moves in.

Picture opening the city gate and letting it walk out, like a guest who stayed too long, and breathe out as it goes. If you pray, join your palms for a moment in the quieter street it leaves.
Nagar, a city: Sohila's fourth hymn, the body crowded with desire and anger, the thorn of ego inside, and the holy company that clears the streets.
Your line: clear the city. Good company does what force alone can't. Until tomorrow, then.

432.title: Hymn 5, sound: karau benantee
432.hook: karau benantee sunahu mere meetaa (Gauri Purbi M5, ang 13)
432.howItsDone: This is the fifth and final hymn of Kirtan Sohila, which Sikhs recite each night before sleep; in gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is then laid to rest for the night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nagar, the city full of thieves; your line was clear the city. Today, Sohila's last hymn.

There's a tone people use when something really matters. Not a speech, not a lecture. A friend leaning across the table, lowering their voice: listen, can I ask you something? It's the tone that gets a phone put down. The last hymn of Sohila opens in that voice. After the crowded city of the fourth hymn, the fifth doesn't raise its voice at all. It turns to the listener, calls them friend, and asks for attention. And it's a third Guru's voice: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru.
screen: `LISTEN, CAN I ASK YOU SOMETHING?` → `THE LAST HYMN LOWERS ITS VOICE.` → `A THIRD GURU: GURU ARJAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line: karau benantee, sunahu mere meetaa. Word by word. Karau: I make, I offer. Benantee: a humble request, a plea; the everyday Punjabi word benti means the same, a heartfelt request. Sunahu: listen. Mere: my. Meetaa: friends. So: I make a request; listen, my friends. Notice who's speaking to whom. Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth, the scripture Sikhs now honor as the Guru Granth Sahib. He could have opened with authority. Instead he opens like someone asking a favor, and calls the listeners friends, not followers. Then the line goes on, and the request turns out to be urgent. In paraphrase: this is the time to serve the holy. We'll open that tomorrow. For now, see the shape Sohila has built. Five hymns, three Gurus. Guru Nanak wrote the first three: the house of praise, the six schools and one sun, the sky's aarti. Guru Ram Das wrote the fourth, the city full of thieves. Guru Arjan wrote this fifth. The first is in a form of Raag Gauri, the second in Asa, the third in Dhanasri, and the last two share Gauri Purbi. A little anthology in one night prayer, ending not with a doctrine but with a friend saying: please, listen.
screen: `KARAU BENANTEE: I MAKE A REQUEST.` · `SUNAHU MERE MEETAA: LISTEN, FRIENDS.` · `FRIENDS, NOT FOLLOWERS.` · `FIVE HYMNS, THREE GURUS.` · then, large: `KARAU BENANTEE.`

segments.voice: Say the line once in an ordinary voice: karau benantee, sunahu mere meetaa. Sit and imagine it said to you, by someone who wants good for you, and if you pray, say Waheguru once, softly.

433.title: Now is the time
433.hook: listen, friends: now is the time to serve the holy and earn the Name (Gauri Purbi M5, ang 13)
433.tomorrow: A wedding song at a funeral
433.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn as the last of Kirtan Sohila every night, so its call that now is the time to serve and remember is often the final teaching heard before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, benti, a humble request; your line was karau benantee. Today, what the request actually is.

A caravan halts at a market town. For a few days there's buying and selling, haggling and loading, and then the caravan moves on. Everyone knows the rule: what you earn here is what you carry home. Spend the market days sleeping, gambling or arguing, and you go home with empty bags. When the last hymn of Sohila explains its urgent request, it reaches for that language: profit, earning, buying, a short stay.
screen: `A MARKET TOWN, A SHORT STAY.` → `WHAT YOU EARN, YOU CARRY HOME.` → `THE HYMN SPEAKS LIKE A TRADER.`

segments.voice: Here's the request, in paraphrase. Listen, my friends: this is the time to serve the holy. Earn the profit of God here, and your dwelling hereafter will be easy. The word for profit is laahaa, an ordinary trader's word, the gain at the end of the day. Then the urgency. In paraphrase again: day and night, life is running down; O mind, meet the Guru and set your affairs in order. Anyone with a deadline understands that: the hours go whether you use them or not. The hymn goes on: this world is caught in corruption and doubt; the one who knows God crosses over. Buy what you came here to buy. Through the Guru, God comes to dwell in the mind, and you reach your own true home in ease, with no more coming and going. Then the very last request in all of Sohila. In paraphrase: Nanak, Your servant, begs for this happiness: make me the dust of the feet of the holy. So the night prayer ends on humility, the lowest place in the room, chosen on purpose. Here's why it belongs at bedtime. Night is when you count the day. What did I earn? Not money: kindness, attention, remembering. The hymn doesn't scold. It just says the market's still open. Now is the time.

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind, someone at home, someone you owe a thank-you, and one small kindness you could give them tonight: a filled water glass, a note, three warm words, a dish washed that isn't yours. Picture yourself giving it, and let that be the day's profit. If you pray, say Waheguru once.

434.title: A wedding song at a funeral
434.hook: Sohila is also sung at cremations, a song of the soul going home
434.howItsDone: At a Sikh cremation, once the pyre is lit, the sangat recites Kirtan Sohila and then the Ardas, as the Sikh Rehat Maryada directs; the same hymns are said by Sikhs every night before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was what did I earn today. It's a week's end too: the sky's aarti, the wind, the city of thieves, Guru Arjan's request. Today, where else Sohila is sung.
screen: `WHAT DID I EARN TODAY.` · `A WEEK: THE AARTI, THE CITY, THE REQUEST.`

segments.voice: A first-dance song at a graveside would stop a room cold. Yet at a Sikh cremation, once the fire is lit, the words recited sound, to anyone who knows them, like a wedding: the date written, oil poured at the threshold, friends asked for their blessings, a bride called to meet her Lord. It's Sohila, the same five hymns said at bedtime. Here the wedding words aren't a mistake. They're the point.
screen: `WEDDING MUSIC, FUNERAL MUSIC.` → `AT THE CREMATION: SOHILA.` → `THE SAME FIVE HYMNS AS LAST NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, sets out the funeral. The body is washed and dressed, and the family gathers. At the cremation ground, once the pyre is lit, the sangat recites Kirtan Sohila, and then the Ardas is said. In the days that follow, a reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib is begun, at home or at a gurdwara. Sikh teaching also asks mourners not to give way to loud wailing. Grief is real, and tears are human, but the songs are of praise. So why Sohila? Go back to its first hymn. The date has been written. Friends, pour the oil, give your blessings, so I may meet my Lord. The summons goes to every house, every day. Read at the pyre, the funeral becomes the day that summons arrives for one soul, and the wedding is the meeting with the Beloved. In the hymn's language, the person who has died isn't lost to darkness. They're going home, the way a bride goes to her new home. And if the same five hymns are sung at bedtime and at the end of a life, some readers hear every night as a small rehearsal: lying down, letting go of the day, trusting the morning to the One. The last line of Sohila, sung at the pyre as at the pillow, is Guru Arjan asking to be the dust of the holy's feet. Even at the end, humility.
screen: `THE PYRE IS LIT; SOHILA IS SUNG.` · `PRAISE INSTEAD OF WAILING.` · `THE SUMMONS ARRIVES FOR ONE SOUL.` · `EVERY NIGHT, A SMALL REHEARSAL.` · then, large: `GOING HOME.`

segments.voice: Let one person who has died come to mind, a grandparent, a friend, a neighbor, and picture their face on a good day, with one kindness, one habit, one laugh of theirs. If grief comes, let it come; nothing needs fixing. Hold them like a friend at the door wishing a traveler well, and if you pray, say Waheguru for them, softly.
Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct that sets out the funeral: Kirtan Sohila is sung there as well as at bedtime, the soul as a bride, called to meet the Beloved and going home.
Your line: going home. Praise and trust, at the end of a day and of a life. Day four hundred thirty-four.
